title: 5 out of 5 Isn't 100%
intro: Five engineers completed the new export flow: “100% success”. The 95% confidence interval was 48–100%.

learn.title: What the interval does
learn.text:
It turns “trust me” into a range, and shifts the conversation from “is five participants significant?” to **“how much risk can we accept?”**

Same task, more data:

• 5 test participants: 100% — 95% CI **48–100%**
• ~45 engineers (analytics): 93% — 95% CI **83–100%**

The estimate barely moved. The interval narrowed from 52 points to 17.

try.q: Five of five participants succeeded. What does the interval tell you?
options: The true rate could be anywhere from about half to all
The task has a 100% success rate
The sample was too small to analyse

learn.title: Which method for which measure
learn.text:
**Task completion** is binary, so use the **Wilson score interval** — it behaves properly at 0% and 100%, where simpler formulas break.

Enter 1 or 0 per participant, take the average and the count, pick z (1.645 for 90%, 1.96 for 95%) and apply the formula. Calabro shares a spreadsheet version.

**Time on task** is skewed, so use a **log-normal** approach instead.

try.q: Which interval method suits task completion?
try.explain: It behaves at the extremes, where simpler formulas break down.

learn.title: Error bars change the conversation
learn.text:
Put the interval on the chart.

A false-alert rate of **12%** sounds minor. The same finding as **9–15% across traders, with some well above average**, changes the priority.

And for new users, a realistic completion benchmark is around **90%** — not 100%. Aiming for perfection in the numbers usually means the measurement is wrong.

try.q: Why put error bars on the chart?
options: The range changes how people prioritise
try.explain: “12%” and “9–15%, some well above” lead to different decisions.

test.q: What does a confidence interval replace?
What happened when the sample grew from 5 to about 45?
options: The interval narrowed sharply; the estimate barely moved
Both the estimate and the interval changed
The estimate rose and the interval widened

test.q: Why not use a simple formula at 100% completion?
options: It breaks down at the extremes
It assumes a normal distribution of time
test.explain: Wilson is designed to behave at 0% and 100%.

test.q: What is a realistic completion benchmark for new users?
test.explain: Perfection in the numbers usually means a measurement problem.
